::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## The decision this serves
Whether this field is the one you want — and, if it is, what to do in the next
twelve months so that someone will pay you to do it.
:::

## 1. What the field actually is

Quantitative pharmacology is the discipline of writing pharmacology as
mathematics so that it can make predictions, and using those predictions to
make decisions about drugs under uncertainty.

That is the whole thing. Everything else — the software, the acronyms, the
regulatory guidances — is machinery in service of one loop:

> **observe → model → predict → decide → observe again**

A useful test of whether you are doing quantitative pharmacology or just doing
mathematics near a drug: *name the decision*. If you cannot say which choice
your model changes — this dose or that one, this trial design or that one,
go or no-go, label this population or exclude it — you are curve-fitting.
Every lesson on this site opens by naming the decision for exactly this reason.

### The vocabulary problem, stated plainly

The names overlap, they are used inconsistently between companies, and nobody
is going to fix this. Here is the honest map:

| Term | What people usually mean | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Quantitative pharmacology** | The whole field: any mathematical modeling of drug action used for decisions | The broadest term. Common as a department name. |
| **Pharmacometrics** | Data-driven modeling of clinical data, especially population PK/PD | The most common job title. In practice ≈ PopPK/PD + exposure–response. |
| **Clinical pharmacology** | The clinical discipline; includes but is wider than modeling | Often the department that *contains* the modelers. Frequently MD/PharmD-led. |
| **PK/PD modeling** | Structural models linking exposure to effect | The core craft, used everywhere. |
| **PBPK** | Physiologically based PK — mechanistic, whole-body | Its own sub-specialty, own software, own regulatory track. |
| **QSP** | Quantitative systems pharmacology — mechanistic models of biology and disease | Closer to systems biology; used earlier, less regulated. |
| **MIDD** | Model-informed drug development | Not a method — a *framework* for how models enter decisions. A regulatory term. |
| **M&S** | Modeling and simulation | Generic umbrella, common in job ads and SOPs. |

You will see all of these on job descriptions, sometimes in the same one. Do not
read too much into the label; read the responsibilities.

## 2. The four questions

Almost every model in this field is answering one of four questions, and it
helps enormously to know which one you are on.

1. **How much drug gets where, and when?** — pharmacokinetics. Absorption,
   distribution, metabolism, excretion, expressed as rates.
2. **What does it do there?** — pharmacodynamics. Target engagement, biomarker
   movement, clinical effect, toxicity.
3. **How much does that differ between people, and why?** — variability.
   Body size, organ function, genetics, co-medication, adherence, and the large
   remainder we cannot explain.
4. **How sure are we?** — uncertainty. Parameter uncertainty, structural
   uncertainty, and the honest gap between "the model says" and "we know".

Beginners are usually taught (1) and (2), get good at them, and then discover
that in industry the value is concentrated in (3) and (4). Variability is why
we need population models at all; uncertainty is why a decision-maker needs you
in the room rather than a spreadsheet.

## 3. The modeling families, and how to choose between them

There is no ranking here. Each family buys you something specific and costs you
something specific, and the choice is made by the decision, never by taste or
by what you happen to know.

| Family | What it buys | What it costs | Typical decision |
|---|---|---|---|
| **NCA** — non-compartmental analysis | Assumption-free summary (AUC, C~max~, t~½~) | Cannot extrapolate or simulate | Did exposure go up with dose? Is there a food effect? |
| **Compartmental PK/PD** | A structure you can simulate from | Structural assumptions you must defend | What regimen holds concentration in the target window? |
| **PopPK / PopPD (NLME)** | Variability quantified and partly explained; sparse data usable | Estimation complexity; heavy diagnostics | Does renal impairment need a dose adjustment in the label? |
| **PBPK** | Extrapolation to untested situations from physiology | Many parameters from *in vitro* work; platform must be qualified | What happens if this is co-dosed with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor, without running the study? |
| **QSP** | Mechanism at the level of biology; hypothesis testing about pathways | Identifiability problems; heavy assumptions | Which target, which combination, which patient subgroup? |
| **MBMA** — model-based meta-analysis | The competitive landscape as a model | Aggregate data, publication bias | Is our effect size worth a phase 3? |
| **CTS** — clinical trial simulation | Design performance under assumptions | Only as good as the assumptions | How many patients, which endpoint, which interim rule? |
| **Bayesian / hierarchical** | Honest uncertainty; prior information used properly | Computation; prior justification | What do we believe after a small phase 1b? |
| **ML / SciML** | Pattern discovery, fast surrogates, hybrid mechanistic-empirical models | Extrapolates badly; hard to defend to a regulator | Which of 200 candidate covariates deserves a mechanistic look? |

A senior modeler's actual skill is mostly *this table*: matching a question to
the cheapest family that can answer it credibly. Reaching for QSP when NCA
would settle the question is as much an error as the reverse.

## 4. Where you sit in drug development

Quantitative pharmacology touches every stage, but the questions change
completely as a molecule moves.

| Stage | The question you are asked | Typical work |
|---|---|---|
| **Discovery** | Which candidate, and what properties does it need? | PK/PD target definition, human dose projection, translational PKPD |
| **IND-enabling** | What is a safe and informative first dose? | Allometric scaling, MABEL/NOAEL translation, PBPK first-in-human prediction |
| **Phase 1** | Does it behave as predicted, and what perturbs it? | SAD/MAD PK, food effect, DDI studies and PBPK predictions, formulation bridging |
| **Phase 2** | What dose, and for whom? | Exposure–response, dose selection, Project Optimus work in oncology |
| **Phase 3** | Does the dosing hold up across the real population? | PopPK for the label, E–R for efficacy and safety, special populations |
| **Filing** | Can you defend all of it? | Summary of Clinical Pharmacology, PopPK and E–R reports, labeling language, responses to agency questions |
| **Post-approval** | What about the populations we did not study? | Pediatric plans, new formulations, real-world dosing, lifecycle commitments |

Two consequences worth internalising early. First, **your deadlines come from
regulatory milestones, not from convergence** — the filing date does not move
because your model did not converge. Second, the same molecule will be modeled
five different ways over ten years by five different people, which is why the
reproducibility habits in `S0-05` are not optional bureaucracy.

### MIDD is a process with a date on it

The table above describes what the work touches. **Model-informed drug
development** is the name for how that work is supposed to enter decisions, and
it is worth knowing that the term is administrative in origin rather than
scientific. Lesko's short perspective ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12699),
free full text) traces the lineage precisely: modelling and simulation had
already been in use for around twenty-five years, ICH E4 gave it context in
1994, and a run of FDA guidances followed — clinical evidence of effectiveness
(1998), population pharmacokinetics (1999), exposure–response (2003), PBPK
(2018). Two publications anchor the intellectual side: Sheiner's *learn versus
confirm* (1997) and Peck and colleagues on what counts as confirmatory evidence
(2003). MIDD itself was **codified in PDUFA VI in 2017**, with a pilot programme
of paired industry–FDA meetings as a performance goal.

Three observations from that piece are more useful to a newcomer than the
chronology:

**Adoption is uneven, and the reasons are organisational.** Lesko reports a wide
gap between companies that use modelling for a single task — empirical dose
selection in early development — and those that use it across the lifecycle. He
attributes the difference to culture, organisational structure and whether
pharmacometrics and biostatistics are aligned or competing for influence, and is
explicit that he does not have validated answers. If your first team does
modelling narrowly, that is a fact about the organisation, not about the field.

**The current toolkit is at a plateau.** Population PK, exposure–response and
PBPK are, in his phrase, where "the easy stuff is done" — which he treats as a
reason to invest in training rather than as bad news. The unexploited areas he
names are real-world data, pharmacoepidemiology, machine learning, and precision
dosing.

**QSP is "technology push", PBPK is "market pull".** This is the sharpest idea in
the paper. PBPK improves something regulators already want; QSP creates interest
in capability regulators have not asked for. That asymmetry, not model quality,
explains much of why QSP submissions have grown while their influence on
approval decisions remains hard to trace. `S4` builds QSP models; this is the
context in which they will be received.

And a line worth keeping: MIDD is a **"team sport"**, and the constraint is
usually communication to decision-makers rather than the modelling itself —
which is why `S0-06` and the Mehrotra & Gobburu tutorial sit where they do in
this curriculum.

## 5. What the job is actually like

The honest version, which recruiters will not tell you:

- **A large fraction of the work is data.** Assembling, checking, reconciling
  and documenting the analysis dataset routinely takes longer than the
  modeling. People who find this beneath them do not become good at this job.
- **The model is not the deliverable.** The deliverable is a decision, a report,
  and a defensible answer to "how do you know?" A beautiful model that nobody
  acts on has produced nothing.
- **You will usually be the only person in the room who understands the
  analysis.** That is real influence and real responsibility. It also means
  your explanation *is* the evidence for everyone else — which is why
  communication sits in the competency list alongside mathematics.
- **Most of your models will be wrong in ways that do not matter, and a few
  will be wrong in ways that do.** Learning to tell which is which is the
  actual expertise, and it takes years.
- **It is a small field.** A few thousand people worldwide do this seriously.
  Your reputation travels, conferences matter more than they do in larger
  disciplines, and being generous with juniors compounds.

## 6. The skill ladder

Four levels. These are not job titles — titles vary wildly — but they map well
onto what people can actually do.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
### L1 · Literate
Can read a modeling report and know what the plots claim. Knows the vocabulary,
can ask a sharp question in a meeting, does not confuse a VPC with a goodness-of-fit
plot. **Evidence:** you can explain someone else's analysis to a third person and
name its weakest assumption.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
### L2 · Practitioner
Can run a defined analysis end to end under supervision: assemble the dataset,
fit the model somebody specified, produce the standard diagnostics, write the
section. **Evidence:** you have completed a full analysis where someone else
chose the approach — and it survived review.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
### L3 · Independent
Chooses the approach, defends it, owns a compound's modeling strategy, knows
when the data cannot answer the question. Speaks to regulators. **Evidence:**
you have said "this analysis will not answer that question" to a senior person
and been right.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
### L4 · Strategic
Shapes programme and regulatory strategy, invents or adapts methods, mentors,
and is trusted when the model and the intuition disagree. **Evidence:** decisions
worth tens of millions have moved because of your analysis, and you can name
the ones where you were wrong.
:::

Most people reach L2 in a year of focused work, L3 in three to five years of
real programmes, and L4 — if at all — after a decade. The step that stalls
people is **L2 → L3**, and it stalls almost always for non-technical reasons:
never having owned a decision, never having been in front of a regulator, never
having had to say no.

## 7. The six competencies

```
                 pharmacology & physiology
                            ▲
   communication  ◀─────────┼─────────▶  mathematics & statistics
                            │
   drug development  ◀──────┼──────▶  computing & data engineering
                            ▼
                    scientific judgement
```

Almost nobody is strong in all six. The people who become genuinely valuable are
usually strong in two technical competencies and then deliberately close the gap
on **drug development context** and **communication** — because those two are
what convert a correct analysis into an actual decision, and they are the two
that self-taught modelers most often skip.

## 8. Where you are coming from, and what you must close

| Background | You already have | Close this gap first |
|---|---|---|
| **PharmD / pharmacy** | Drug knowledge, clinical context, credibility with clinicians | Calculus and differential equations; programming beyond spreadsheets; statistics |
| **Chemical / biomedical engineering** | ODEs, numerics, transport, systems thinking | Pharmacology and physiology; clinical trial reality; regulatory context |
| **Statistics / mathematics** | Estimation, inference, uncertainty, study design | Biology and mechanism; why a mechanistic structure beats a flexible fit here |
| **Biology / pharmacology PhD** | Mechanism, target biology, experimental judgement | Mathematics and computing — usually the largest gap, and the most closable |
| **Data science / CS** | Programming, workflow, ML, scale | Pharmacology; small-*n* thinking; why extrapolation matters more than prediction accuracy |
| **MD** | Interpretation, clinical relevance, enormous credibility | Computing and formal modeling; time |

The gap is closable in every row. What is not closable by self-study is
**drug development context** — that one requires being near real programmes,
which is why the job-search section below matters as much as the study plan.

## 9. How to become one — a twelve-month route

This assumes five to eight hours a week and no prior modeling experience. It is
deliberately narrow: one language, one method family, one finished analysis.
Breadth comes later and comes easily; depth does not.

**Months 1–2 · Foundations.** Work `S0-01` through `S0-06` on this site. By the
end you should be able to write a two-compartment model as ODEs, simulate it,
explain why every parameter in an oral dataset carries a `/F`, and assemble a
dataset that a fitting engine will accept without complaint.
*Non-negotiable outcome:* one language you are fluent in — R or Python, not both.

**Months 3–4 · PK/PD core.** Strand `S1`. NCA, compartmental models, absorption,
nonlinear elimination, E~max~ and exposure–response. Simulate before you fit —
every parameter you can move by hand is a parameter you will later understand
when an estimate looks wrong.
*Non-negotiable outcome:* you can predict the shape of a profile before running
the code, and you are usually right.

**Months 5–8 · Population modeling.** Strand `S2`, the longest stretch and the
one that makes you employable. Mixed effects, an estimation method you can
explain, covariate modeling, and the full diagnostic battery. Use `CASE-SM` and
grade yourself against `truth.yml` — you will not get another chance in your
career to compare your estimates against the real values.
*Non-negotiable outcome:* one complete PopPK analysis, from raw data to a
written report, that a stranger could reproduce from your repository.

**Months 9–10 · Pick one specialisation.** PBPK (`S3`) if you like physiology
and *in vitro* data; QSP (`S4`) if you like biology and systems; Bayesian
methods (`S5`) if you like inference. One, not three.

**Months 11–12 · Decisions and communication.** Strand `S6`, plus `S7`. Take
your months 5–8 analysis and turn it into a fifteen-minute presentation for a
non-modeler and a written report for a reviewer. Then present it to a real
audience — a lab meeting, a local chapter, a conference poster.
*Non-negotiable outcome:* something public with your name on it.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## The five non-negotiables
Everything above compresses to five things. If you have all five, you are
employable at L2; if you are missing any, you are not, whatever else you know.

1. **One language, fluently** — you never fight the tool.
2. **One NLME engine** you can drive end to end.
3. **One complete analysis** — raw data to written conclusion, not a notebook.
4. **One written report** in the shape the industry actually uses.
5. **One public artefact** — a repository, a poster, a talk. Certificates lose
   to a reproducible analysis every time.
:::

### What the twelve months can be built from, at zero cost

Every item below was checked and is free; the full set is on the
[Resources](../../resources.qmd) page.

| Need | Free resource |
|---|---|
| Clinical pharmacology grounding | [NIH *Principles of Clinical Pharmacology*](https://ocreco.od.nih.gov/courses/principles-clinical-pharmacology) — 48 recorded lectures, publicly viewable |
| A full pharmacometrics curriculum | [Metrum Open Courseware](https://metrumrg.com/courses/) — fifteen courses under CC BY, no login: R for pharmacometrics, population PK/PD, Bayesian, mrgsolve |
| Structured course with a cohort | [Pharmacometrics Africa](https://pmxafrica.org/moodle/) — open-access self-paced course in English and French, free registration |
| Pharmacology fundamentals | [MIT OCW HST.151](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/hst-151-principles-of-pharmacology-spring-2005/) — notes, problem sets and exams with solutions, CC BY-NC-SA |
| Software | [nlmixr2](https://nlmixr2.org/), [mrgsolve](https://mrgsolve.org/), [PK-Sim/MoBi](https://www.open-systems-pharmacology.org/) — see `S0-04` |
| What the field is arguing about | [PAGE abstract archive](https://www.page-meeting.org/) — every abstract since 1992, free to browse |
| What regulators expect | The 26 guidances on [Resources](../../resources.qmd) — all free, most short |

There is no paywall between you and this job. There is a time cost, and it is
large, but the materials are not the constraint.

## 10. Getting the first job

**Where the roles are.** Large pharma (deepest specialisation, most process);
biotech (broader scope, less support, faster); CROs and consultancies (highest
volume and variety of compounds — an excellent, underrated first job); regulators
(FDA, EMA, PMDA — outstanding training and a strong CV line); software vendors
(Certara, Simulations Plus, Metrum, Pumas-AI); academia (methods and teaching).

**Titles to search.** Pharmacometrician · Clinical Pharmacology Modeler ·
PKPD Scientist · Quantitative Pharmacologist · Modeling & Simulation Scientist ·
PBPK Scientist · QSP Scientist · Quantitative Clinical Pharmacologist.

**What interviews actually test.** In practice, three things:

1. *Can you reason about a profile?* You will be shown a concentration–time plot
   or a diagnostic and asked what it means. Practise this out loud.
2. *Have you finished something?* One complete analysis you can walk through
   beats five half-projects.
3. *Can you explain it to a non-modeler?* Frequently the deciding factor, and
   the one candidates prepare for least.

**Highest-yield moves, in order.**

- Present a poster at ACoP or PAGE. The field is small enough that this works.
  Nowhere else can you meet most of your future hiring managers in three days.
- Do a fellowship or internship: FDA ORISE, industry postdoctoral fellowships
  (several large sponsors run two-year programmes), ISoP student programmes.
- Publish your `CASE-SM` analysis publicly, with the code, and put the link in
  your CV. Almost no applicant does this.
- Answer questions in the community — the ISoP forum, this site's threads.
  Being visibly helpful and visibly correct is a hiring signal.
- Learn the regulatory vocabulary before your first interview. Reading two
  approved Summary of Clinical Pharmacology reviews on Drugs@FDA will teach you
  more about what the job produces than any course.

## 11. After L3: the forks

- **Individual contributor / principal scientist** — deepest science, stays
  hands-on, becomes the person consulted across programmes.
- **Manager and functional leader** — builds and defends the group; hands-on
  time drops sharply, and pretending otherwise is the classic new-manager error.
- **Methodologist** — develops methods and software, usually with academic
  collaborations and a publication record.
- **Regulator** — the widest view of the field in existence; you will see
  hundreds of programmes rather than five.
- **Consultant** — variety, exposure, and the fastest route to seniority through
  sheer number of compounds touched.
- **Academic** — trains the next generation; note that this field's academic
  positions are heavily concentrated in a handful of programmes.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Failure modes — the three ways beginners stall
**Learning the tool before the model.** People spend six months on NONMEM
control-stream syntax without being able to sketch what the model does. The
symptom is being unable to predict what happens to the curve if you double
`ka`. The fix is simulation: change a parameter by hand, look at the picture,
before you ever estimate anything.

**Never finishing.** A folder of half-analyses is worth less than one complete,
mediocre analysis with a written conclusion. Finishing is a separate skill from
modeling, and it is the one employers screen on.

**Only ever working with clean data.** Textbook datasets have no duplicated
records, no impossible timestamps, no units changing halfway through, no BLQ
values and no missing doses. Real ones have all of these at once. `CASE-SM`
deliberately includes below-quantification samples and four covariates that do
nothing, because the skill being taught is discrimination, not fitting.
:::

## Check yourself

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. A colleague says "we don't need a model, we have the phase 1 data." When are they right?
When the decision is inside the range of what was directly observed and does not
require extrapolation across dose, population, regimen or time. If the phase 1
study measured exactly the regimen you are asking about, in the population you
are asking about, NCA and a plot may genuinely be enough — and reaching for a
model anyway is the error described in section 3. They are wrong the moment the
question involves a population you did not study, a regimen you did not test, or
a probability rather than a point estimate.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Why is variability a *first-class* object here, rather than noise to average away?
Because doses are given to individuals, not to means. A regimen that is optimal
on average can be toxic in the top decile of exposure and useless in the bottom.
The entire population-modeling apparatus exists to separate variability we can
explain and dose-adjust for (body size, organ function, co-medication) from
variability we cannot, and to quantify what remains — which is exactly what a
label's dosing section has to survive.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. You have twelve months and a full-time job. What is the single highest-value output?
One complete, public, reproducible analysis with a written report — not a
certificate, not a broad survey of five methods. It simultaneously demonstrates
the language, the engine, the workflow, the judgement and the communication,
which is the entire L2 checklist in one artefact. Everything else in section 9
is scaffolding for producing it.
:::

## Going further

- **Next on this path:** [S0-01 · Compartments and ODEs from first principles](../s0-01-compartments-and-odes/) — where the equations behind everything above come from.
- **If you are here to read, not to build:** skip to
  [S0-06 · Reading a model report](../s0-06-reading-a-model-report/), then come back.
- **External:** the ISoP discussion forum for practitioner questions; Drugs@FDA
  for real Summary of Clinical Pharmacology reviews; the FDA and EMA guidances on
  population PK, exposure–response and PBPK, which are short, readable and
  tell you exactly what the deliverable looks like.

*Seen in the wild:* the most common reason a modeling result fails to change a
decision is not that the model was wrong. It is that the analysis arrived after
the decision was made. Timing is a technical skill in this job.
